processing: Black tea in the gongfu manner: withered, rolled, fully oxidised and dried. Little is documented about any special local steps.
harvest_season: Not well documented; as with other Chinese gongfu blacks, spring leaf is usually preferred.
appearance_dry: Tight, fine strands, glossy dark with visible tips.
taste_profile: A fresh, lasting aroma and a sweet, mellow taste.

brewing.notes: Ordinary gongfu black settings; nothing specific to this tea is recorded.

vintage_note: As usual for gongfu black teas, it is sold as current or recent harvest tea, with no established ageing market on record. Ask for the picking year and producer, since the name leans heavily on history.
description:
He Hong takes its name from Hekou, an old river port in Yanshan county in northeast Jiangxi. It is as much a trade name as a tea: black tea from the wider Wuyi hinterland passed through the Hekou docks and shipped out under this label.

Today's tea is made in Yanshan by the usual black tea method. Little is documented about specific local techniques, so assume the normal sequence of withering, rolling, oxidation and drying rather than anything unique.

Descriptions give tight, glossy strands, a bright red liquor, a fresh aroma and a mellow sweetness. Those are also the words used for many good Chinese blacks, so taste it for yourself, in short gaiwan steeps with hot water.

Be cautious about grand labels. Claims that it is the ancestor of all Chinese black tea are promotional. A clear producer, county and harvest year say more about what is in the bag.
history:
Hekou was a major trading town on the Ming and Qing river routes, promoted today as a leading stop on the Tea Road to Russia: tea from around Wuyi moved through its docks north via Jiujiang and Wuchang, and on through Zhangjiakou and Mongolia, or south towards Guangzhou.

A Ming origin for He Hong and its title as the first Chinese black tea are repeated in local and travel writing, but firm historical evidence is thin, and both should be read as local tradition.
